title: The Cambrian Explosion
text:
Roughly 540 million years ago, over a span of perhaps 20 million years, the fossil record shifts abruptly. Before this interval, most preserved organisms are simple and soft-bodied. After it, nearly every major animal body plan alive today appears, many with hard shells, jointed limbs and complex eyes. Palaeontologists call this the Cambrian explosion.

Explanations remain contested. One proposal points to a rise in atmospheric oxygen, which would have permitted the higher metabolic rates that active predation demands. Another emphasises ecology: once one lineage evolved effective predation, the pressure to develop armour and speed would have cascaded through every other lineage. A third argues the explosion is partly an illusion of preservation, since hard parts fossilise far more readily than soft tissue, and earlier soft-bodied ancestors may simply have left no trace.

options: To trace the evolution of the eye across geological time
To compare fossil preservation in marine and terrestrial settings
To describe a rapid diversification of animal life and the competing accounts of it
To argue that the Cambrian explosion never actually occurred
questions.explanation: The passage first defines the Cambrian explosion, then presents three explanations. It does not settle the question, so it is descriptive rather than argumentative.

questions.question: According to the passage, higher atmospheric oxygen would have mattered because it
options: allowed the faster metabolism that active hunting requires
questions.explanation: The passage states that rising oxygen would have permitted the higher metabolic rates that active predation demands.

questions.question: The word illusion in the passage is closest in meaning to
questions.explanation: The third explanation suggests the explosion may only seem sudden because soft-bodied ancestors did not fossilise. That is a misleading appearance, not an intentional deception.

title: Why Venice Is Sinking
text:
Venice is subsiding, and the causes are both natural and human. The city rests on wooden piles driven into soft lagoon sediment, which compacts slowly under load. This natural settling would amount to only a few centimetres per century.

The twentieth century accelerated matters sharply. Industrial wells on the mainland drew groundwater from beneath the lagoon, and as the aquifer drained, the sediment above it compressed. Between 1930 and 1970 the city sank roughly twelve centimetres, several times the natural rate. Pumping was banned in the 1970s and subsidence slowed almost immediately, though the compaction already suffered cannot be reversed.

Meanwhile the sea itself is rising. The practical threat to Venice is therefore the sum of two movements, one of the land and one of the water, neither large alone.

questions.explanation: The final sentence states that the threat is the sum of two movements, neither large on its own.

questions.explanation: The passage gives twelve centimetres over that period, described as several times the natural rate.

title: The Domestication of Fire
text:
When early humans gained control of fire is among the most disputed questions in archaeology. Claims for controlled use at Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa reach back a million years, based on burnt bone and ash found deep inside the cave, far from any opening lightning could have reached.

Sceptics note that distinguishing a managed hearth from a natural burn is difficult. Ash can be washed into a cave; bone can be charred by a wildfire and later carried in by scavengers. Convincing evidence requires a repeated pattern: hearths in the same spot across many layers, stone arranged around them, and heat-cracked rock.

Such unambiguous evidence becomes common only around 400,000 years ago, which some read as the true threshold and others as the point at which the evidence merely became durable enough to survive.

options: To show the cave was difficult to reach
To argue that lightning is a common ignition source
To suggest the fire is unlikely to have been natural
To explain how the cave was excavated
questions.explanation: Its distance from an opening makes ignition by lightning implausible, which is why the location supports controlled use.

questions.explanation: The passage lists repeated hearths in the same spot across layers, arranged stone and heat-cracked rock.

options: the earliest claim anyone has made
universally accepted as the origin of fire use
questions.explanation: The final sentence gives two readings: a true threshold, or the point at which evidence became durable.

title: Why Leaves Change Colour
text:
The yellows and oranges of autumn are not manufactured in autumn. Carotenoid pigments are present in the leaf throughout the growing season, masked by the far more abundant green of chlorophyll. As days shorten, the tree withdraws nitrogen and other nutrients from its leaves, chlorophyll breaks down and is not replaced, and the carotenoids beneath are revealed.

Reds behave differently. Anthocyanins are synthesised fresh in autumn, which is puzzling, since a tree about to shed its leaves is spending energy on a pigment it will discard. One hypothesis is sunscreen: anthocyanins may shield the leaf from light damage while nutrients are being recovered. Another suggests the red signals to insects that the tree is well defended. Neither explanation is settled, and the two are not mutually exclusive.

questions.explanation: Carotenoids are present all season and become visible once chlorophyll is no longer replaced.

title: The Standardisation of Time
text:
Before the railways, time was local. Each town set its clocks by the sun, so noon in one city fell several minutes from noon in the next. For travellers on foot or horseback the discrepancy was invisible.

Railways made it intolerable. A train crossing several towns in an afternoon had to publish a timetable, and a timetable in dozens of local times was an invitation to collision. British railway companies adopted a single standard, Greenwich time, from the 1840s, decades before Parliament made it official. In North America the railroads divided the continent into time zones themselves in 1883, again ahead of any legislation.

In both cases a private industry imposed a public standard because its own operations demanded one, and governments ratified afterwards what had already become practice.

questions.explanation: Both examples show railways imposing a standard that legislation only later confirmed.

options: Travel was too slow for the discrepancy to matter

questions.explanation: The passage says the discrepancy was invisible to travellers on foot or horseback.

questions.explanation: Governments confirmed in law what industry had already adopted.

title: Coral Bleaching
text:
A reef-building coral is two organisms living as one. The coral animal provides shelter; single-celled algae living in its tissue provide most of its food through photosynthesis, and give the reef its colour.

The partnership is temperature-sensitive. When water warms even one or two degrees above the summer maximum for a sustained period, the algae produce compounds that damage the host, and the coral expels them. What remains is white skeleton visible through transparent tissue, which is why the event is called bleaching. A bleached coral is not dead. If cooler water returns quickly, algae can recolonise the tissue and the coral recovers.

What has changed is frequency. Bleaching events once separated by decades now recur within a few years, and reefs are increasingly struck again before they have finished recovering from the last.

unable to feed at any point
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly says a bleached coral is not dead and can recover if cooler water returns.

questions.explanation: Warming causes the algae to produce compounds that damage the host.

options: Bleaching has become more severe in each event

questions.explanation: The last paragraph emphasises frequency: reefs are hit again before recovery finishes.

title: The Origins of Paper Money
text:
Paper money began as a receipt. Merchants in Tang dynasty China, reluctant to haul strings of copper coin across the country, deposited them with trusted agents and carried a written certificate instead, redeemable at the other end. The paper had value only because the coin behind it did.

Under the Song, the state noticed that most certificates circulated for long periods without being redeemed. If holders were content to trade the paper itself, the issuer could print somewhat more of it than the metal on deposit. Handled cautiously this expanded the money supply usefully. Handled otherwise it produced the first paper inflations in recorded history, and by the thirteenth century some issues had lost nearly all their purchasing power.

The mechanism and its temptation have not changed since.

questions.explanation: The passage says the paper had value only because the coin behind it did.

questions.explanation: The state noticed most certificates circulated for long periods without being redeemed.

questions.explanation: Saying the mechanism and its temptation have not changed implies modern issuers face the same incentive.

title: How Vaccines Train the Immune System
text:
The immune system responds to a first infection slowly. Days pass while the body identifies the pathogen and multiplies the few cells that happen to recognise it, and during that delay the infection spreads.

A vaccine exploits memory. It presents a harmless version of the pathogen, or a distinctive fragment of one, so the body mounts a response with no disease to accompany it. Afterwards a population of memory cells persists, sometimes for decades. On genuine exposure the response begins in hours rather than days, often before the person notices symptoms.

Protection is rarely absolute. Some vaccines prevent infection outright; others allow infection but blunt its severity. And where a pathogen mutates rapidly in the region the immune system recognises, memory built against one variant may only partly transfer to the next.

questions.question: What is the central advantage a vaccine provides?
options: It shortens the delay before an effective response
It eliminates the need for memory cells
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts a slow first response with a response that begins in hours after vaccination.

options: must be repeated every year without exception
reduce severity rather than prevent infection
questions.explanation: The passage states that others allow infection but blunt its severity.

questions.question: Why can memory transfer only partly to a new variant?
options: The pathogen mutates in the recognised region
questions.explanation: Rapid mutation in the region the immune system recognises limits how well memory transfers.

title: Perspective in Renaissance Painting
text:
Linear perspective is a set of rules for making a flat surface read as depth. Lines that recede from the viewer converge on a vanishing point; objects diminish at a calculable rate. Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated the geometry in Florence around 1420, and Leon Battista Alberti set it down in writing a decade later, giving painters a procedure rather than an intuition.

The effect was not merely technical. A perspectival painting implies a single viewer standing at one particular spot, since the geometry only resolves from there. Medieval painting had scaled figures by importance, a saint larger than a merchant regardless of position. Perspective replaced that hierarchy with a uniform space in which size reports distance alone.

What looks like a gain in realism was also a change in what a picture was understood to be about.

questions.explanation: The paragraph argues the gain in realism was also a change in what a picture was about.

questions.explanation: The passage says figures were scaled by importance, a saint larger than a merchant regardless of position.

questions.explanation: The geometry only resolves from one spot, implying a single intended viewer.

title: The Silence of Owl Flight
text:
Most birds make noise in flight because air passing over the wing breaks into turbulence, and turbulence is sound. Owls that hunt by ear cannot afford it: the prey would hear them, and so would they, masking the faint rustle they are listening for.

Three features quiet the wing. A comb-like fringe on the leading edge breaks the oncoming air into fine streams rather than one sheet. A soft trailing fringe lets those streams rejoin gradually instead of shedding abruptly. And a velvety surface over the wing absorbs the remaining high-frequency sound.

The adaptations cost something. The structures add drag and work best at slow speeds, which is why they appear in owls that quarter slowly over open ground and are reduced or absent in fish-eating owls, whose prey cannot hear them coming anyway.

options: Their prey cannot hear an approaching bird
questions.explanation: The passage says fish-eating owls' prey cannot hear them coming anyway.

options: keeps the owl's own hearing unobstructed
questions.explanation: The passage notes noise would mask the faint rustle the owl is listening for.

options: are found in all birds of prey
questions.explanation: The final paragraph states the structures add drag and work best at slow speeds.

title: Writing and the Alphabet
text:
Writing was invented independently perhaps three or four times, but the alphabet appears to have been invented once. Sumerian cuneiform and Chinese characters began as signs for words. Egyptian hieroglyphs included signs for consonant sounds, but retained hundreds of word signs alongside them.

The decisive step came from workers in the Sinai around 1800 BCE who borrowed a small set of Egyptian signs and used them purely for the sounds their Egyptian names began with. A sign for a house, per, came to stand for the sound p. The result needed a few dozen characters rather than several hundred, and every later alphabet, Phoenician, Greek, Latin, Arabic and the Indic scripts, descends from that adaptation.

Why it happened only once is unclear. The idea is simple in hindsight, but it required treating a sign as a sound rather than a thing.

options: using existing signs for their initial sounds
reducing the number of words in a language
questions.explanation: Sinai workers used Egyptian signs purely for the sounds their names began with.

questions.question: What advantage did the alphabet offer?
options: It could record more languages at once
It was faster to carve in stone
questions.explanation: The result needed a few dozen characters rather than several hundred.

questions.question: The passage suggests the invention was difficult because it required
options: treating a sign as a sound rather than a thing
a large population of literate workers
a writing surface that did not exist
questions.explanation: The last sentence identifies exactly this conceptual shift.

title: Sleep and Memory
text:
Sleep does not merely rest the brain; it processes what the waking day supplied. During slow-wave sleep, patterns of neural firing recorded during learning are replayed, and the replay appears to strengthen connections in the cortex where long-term memories reside.

Experiments make the link concrete. Volunteers who learn a sequence of finger movements and then sleep perform measurably better the next morning than volunteers who learn it in the morning and are tested after an equal interval awake. The improvement arrives during sleep rather than with practice.

Selectivity is the interesting part. Not everything is consolidated. Material that participants were told would be tested is retained better than material they believed irrelevant, which suggests the sleeping brain is acting on a decision the waking brain made about what matters.

options: Sleep has no effect on motor skills
Practice in the morning is more effective
Improvement occurs during sleep rather than practice
questions.explanation: Those who slept improved more than those awake for an equal interval, so gain came during sleep.

questions.question: According to the passage, memories are consolidated
questions.explanation: Material expected to be tested was retained better, indicating selectivity.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the sleeping brain
options: acts on priorities set while awake
questions.explanation: The final clause says it acts on a decision the waking brain made about what matters.

title: The Columbian Exchange
text:
The transfer of organisms between the Americas and the rest of the world after 1492 reshaped both. Maize and the potato moved east and raised the ceiling on European and Chinese populations, since both yield more calories per hectare than the grains they supplemented. Cassava did the same across parts of Africa.

Movement in the other direction was more destructive. Smallpox, measles and influenza had circulated in Eurasia for millennia, and populations there carried partial resistance. American populations had none, and mortality in the century after contact reached levels that historians still debate but that were certainly catastrophic.

The exchange was therefore asymmetric in kind rather than in volume: the Americas contributed crops that supported growth, and received diseases that caused collapse.

The exchange moved more species west than east

questions.explanation: The final sentence states the asymmetry in kind: crops one way, disease the other.

options: They had no prior exposure and no partial resistance
questions.explanation: Eurasian populations carried partial resistance from millennia of exposure; American populations had none.

questions.explanation: Both yield more calories per hectare than the grains they supplemented.

title: Why the Sky Is Blue
text:
Sunlight contains all visible wavelengths. When it enters the atmosphere it strikes molecules much smaller than the waves themselves, and those molecules scatter it. The efficiency of this scattering depends steeply on wavelength: shorter waves are scattered far more than longer ones, by a factor that rises as the fourth power of frequency.

Blue and violet are therefore thrown across the sky in every direction, while red passes more directly through. The sky we see is scattered short-wavelength light arriving from everywhere but the sun.

Why blue and not violet, which scatters even more? Partly because sunlight contains less violet to begin with, and partly because the human eye is markedly less sensitive to it. The colour of the sky is a fact about our eyes as much as about the air.

questions.explanation: Scattering efficiency rises steeply for shorter wavelengths.

questions.explanation: The passage gives exactly these two reasons.

questions.explanation: It calls the sky's colour a fact about our eyes as much as about the air.

title: The Economics of Lighthouses
text:
Economists long used the lighthouse as the standard illustration of a public good. Its light cannot be withheld from a passing ship, and one ship's use does not diminish another's. Since no operator could charge for it, the argument ran, only a government would ever build one.

Ronald Coase examined the British record and found the history less tidy. Many early English lighthouses were built by private parties under royal patent, who recovered costs through dues collected at ports, since a ship that had benefited from the light generally had to dock somewhere. The good was non-excludable at sea but the beneficiaries were identifiable on land.

The example survives in textbooks, but Coase's point stands: whether a good must be publicly provided is an empirical question, not one settled by its definition.

options: Lighthouses are not public goods at all
Private parties had in fact financed lighthouses
questions.explanation: Coase found many early English lighthouses were privately built and funded through port dues.

options: Through dues collected when ships docked
By selling the land around the lighthouse
questions.explanation: Dues were collected at ports, since beneficiary ships had to dock somewhere.

options: Coase disproved the concept of a public good

Textbooks should stop using the lighthouse example
All public goods can be privately supplied
questions.explanation: The final sentence states it is an empirical question, not settled by definition.

title: The Deep Scattering Layer
text:
When sonar came into wide use in the 1940s, operators found a puzzling reflection a few hundred metres below the surface, apparently a false sea floor. It rose towards the surface at dusk and sank again at dawn.

The layer turned out to be alive. It consists of small fish, squid and crustaceans whose gas-filled swim bladders reflect sound, and it moves because the animals do. They spend daylight in dark water where predators that hunt by sight cannot easily find them, and rise at night to feed in the productive surface layer.

This is now recognised as the largest migration on earth, undertaken daily by an enormous biomass, and it matters far beyond biology: animals feeding at the surface and excreting at depth carry carbon downward every night.

questions.explanation: The passage says the reflection appeared to be a false sea floor.

options: To avoid predators that hunt by sight

questions.explanation: They spend daylight in dark water where visual predators cannot easily find them.

questions.explanation: Animals feeding at the surface and excreting at depth carry carbon downward.

title: Reading Tree Rings
text:
A temperate tree adds one ring a year: pale, fast-grown wood in spring, dark dense wood late in the season. Counting rings gives an age, but the width of each ring carries more information, since a tree grows wide rings in favourable years and narrow ones in drought.

Because all trees in a region experience the same weather, their ring patterns match. A distinctive sequence of narrow rings in a living tree can be found in the outer rings of an old beam, and in the inner rings of an older beam still. Chaining these overlaps backwards has produced continuous records reaching thousands of years.

The method has limits. Tropical trees growing in constant conditions may add no clear rings at all, and a tree stressed by insects can produce a narrow ring in a wet year.

questions.question: What does the width of a tree ring primarily indicate?
options: How favourable that year's conditions were
questions.explanation: Wide rings form in favourable years, narrow rings in drought.

options: By counting rings in tropical species
By matching overlapping patterns between samples
questions.explanation: Distinctive sequences are matched between living trees and progressively older timber.

questions.question: The passage mentions insect damage in order to
options: explain why tropical trees lack rings
show that ring width can mislead
questions.explanation: A stressed tree can produce a narrow ring in a wet year, a limitation of the method.

title: Why Mars Lost Its Atmosphere
text:
Mars once had liquid water on its surface, which requires an atmosphere thick enough to keep it from boiling away. Today the atmospheric pressure is under one percent of Earth's. Where the air went is largely settled.

Earth is wrapped in a magnetic field generated by motion in its molten core, and that field deflects the solar wind. Mars is smaller, cooled faster, and its core dynamo shut down early. With no field, the solar wind reached the upper atmosphere directly and stripped gas molecules away over hundreds of millions of years. Measurements from orbiting spacecraft have watched the process continuing today and allowed the historical rate to be estimated.

Size, in other words, set the outcome: a smaller planet cooled sooner, lost its dynamo sooner, and lost its air.

questions.question: What ultimately caused Mars to lose its atmosphere?
options: Absorption of gases into the soil
Loss of its magnetic field, exposing the atmosphere to the solar wind
A collision with a large asteroid
questions.explanation: With the dynamo shut down there was no field, and the solar wind stripped the atmosphere.

questions.question: Why did Mars lose its core dynamo before Earth did?
options: It is farther from the sun
It is smaller and cooled faster
questions.explanation: The passage attributes the early shutdown to Mars being smaller and cooling faster.

questions.question: The passage indicates that atmospheric loss on Mars
options: is still occurring and has been measured
questions.explanation: Orbiting spacecraft have watched the process continuing today.

title: The Grid Plan
text:
Laying a city out on a grid is old and widespread. Miletus used one in the fifth century BCE, as did Chinese capitals, Roman colonies and Spanish colonial towns. The pattern recurs because it solves practical problems: land is easy to divide and sell, addresses are easy to find, and a surveyor can extend the plan indefinitely without redesigning it.

The costs are equally consistent. A grid ignores terrain, so San Francisco runs streets straight up hills that a curved road would have climbed gently. It offers no natural centre, since every intersection resembles every other. And it lengthens diagonal journeys, which is why cities with grids often acquire one or two diagonal avenues cut across them at great expense.

The grid is not a failure of imagination but a trade, chosen most often where land had to be distributed quickly.

questions.explanation: It calls the grid not a failure of imagination but a trade.

title: Equal Temperament
text:
Two notes sound consonant when their frequencies form a simple ratio. A perfect fifth is three to two. Tuning a keyboard by stacking pure fifths, however, produces a problem: twelve pure fifths do not land exactly where seven octaves land, but slightly beyond, and the small surplus has to go somewhere.

Earlier systems parked the error in one interval, leaving most keys sweetly in tune and one unusable, so-called wolf interval. Equal temperament instead divides the discrepancy evenly across all twelve semitones. Every fifth is then very slightly narrow, no interval except the octave is pure, and in exchange every key sounds identical in character and a player may modulate freely.

The gain was compositional. Music that travels through many keys, common after Bach, is practical only on an instrument tuned this way.

options: Instruments drifting out of tune with use
Twelve pure fifths not matching seven octaves
questions.explanation: The surplus from stacking pure fifths is the discrepancy that must be distributed.

options: Purity in every interval except the octave
questions.explanation: No interval except the octave is pure once the error is spread evenly.

options: every key sounds alike and modulation is free
questions.explanation: Every key sounds identical in character and a player may modulate freely.

title: Why Ice Floats
text:
Almost every substance is denser as a solid than as a liquid, because cooling slows molecules and lets them pack more closely. Water reverses this, and the reason lies in the shape of its molecule.

Each water molecule can form hydrogen bonds with four neighbours, but only at particular angles. In liquid water these bonds form and break constantly, and molecules slip into whatever gaps appear. On freezing, the bonds lock into a rigid lattice that holds each molecule at the required angle, and that arrangement contains more empty space than the liquid. Ice is therefore about nine percent less dense, and floats.

The consequence is ecological. A lake freezes from the top down, and the ice insulates the water beneath. Were ice denser, lakes would freeze from the bed upward and few temperate aquatic species would survive a winter.

options: Its rigid lattice contains more empty space
questions.explanation: The locked lattice holds molecules at fixed angles and contains more empty space than the liquid.

options: Water would boil at a lower temperature
Lakes would freeze from the bottom upward
questions.explanation: The passage states lakes would freeze from the bed upward.

questions.explanation: It describes the rigid ordered arrangement molecules lock into on freezing.

title: Pompeii and the Problem of Preservation
text:
Pompeii is often called a city frozen in time, but the phrase flatters the evidence. The eruption of 79 CE buried the town in ash, sealing streets, furniture and food, and that seal preserved an ordinary day with a completeness almost nowhere else achieves.

Yet what survives is a town in the middle of repairs. An earthquake seventeen years earlier had damaged many buildings, and a good deal of Pompeii was scaffolded, emptied or abandoned when the ash fell. Some houses were building sites rather than homes.

Excavation added its own distortions. Early digs removed objects without recording where they lay, and material exposed to air after centuries underground decayed quickly. The site is extraordinary evidence, but evidence of a particular disrupted moment, recovered by methods that destroyed part of what they found.

The town was disrupted and partly abandoned when buried

options: it was carried out too slowly

it focused only on public buildings
questions.explanation: Early digs removed objects without recording where they lay.

title: Herd Immunity
text:
A pathogen needs new hosts. If enough of a population is immune, an infected person is likely to meet immune people and the chain of transmission breaks even though susceptible individuals remain. This indirect protection is called herd immunity.

The threshold depends on how contagious the pathogen is. A disease in which each case produces two further cases on average requires about half the population to be immune; measles, where one case can produce twelve, requires roughly ninety-five percent. Small drops in coverage therefore matter far more for highly contagious diseases.

Two assumptions are often overlooked. The calculation supposes immune people are mixed evenly through the population, and clusters of unvaccinated people can sustain outbreaks in a country whose average coverage looks safe. It also supposes immunity lasts, which for some pathogens it does not.

questions.explanation: Infected people mostly meet immune people, so transmission chains break.

options: Each case can produce many further cases
questions.explanation: One measles case can produce twelve, raising the threshold to about ninety-five percent.

questions.question: According to the passage, a country with safe average coverage may still see outbreaks because
questions.explanation: The calculation assumes even mixing; clusters can sustain outbreaks.

title: The Rise of the Novel
text:
The novel is a young form. Long prose fiction existed earlier, but the novel as it is now recognised, following ordinary people through plausible events in a specific time and place, emerged in eighteenth-century Europe alongside conditions that made it viable.

Cheap printing and rising literacy created a readership. Circulating libraries let a reader who could not afford a book borrow one, which made length commercially possible. And a growing middle class supplied both the audience and the subject, since the form takes private life seriously in a way epic and romance had not.

The novel also required a reader willing to spend many solitary hours with invented people. Contemporary critics worried about exactly that, warning that novel reading encouraged idleness and unreal expectations, particularly in young women.

title: Urban Heat Islands
text:
A city is measurably warmer than the countryside around it, often by several degrees at night. Three mechanisms account for most of the difference.

Materials come first. Asphalt and masonry absorb solar energy through the day and release it slowly after dark, so a city cools far more slowly than open ground. Second, cities lack vegetation. A tree cools its surroundings by evaporating water from its leaves, and a paved surface does none of this. Third, cities generate heat directly, from engines, machinery and air conditioning, which cools interiors by moving heat outdoors.

Remedies follow the causes: reflective roofing, street trees, and surfaces that let rain soak in rather than run off. None is expensive relative to a city's budget, and the measured effects are large.

questions.explanation: None is expensive relative to a city's budget, and measured effects are large.

title: Falsifiability
text:
Karl Popper asked what separates science from other systems of belief, and rejected the obvious answer. Confirmation, he argued, is too easy: a theory flexible enough to explain any outcome will find support everywhere, and finding support proves little.

His criterion was falsifiability. A scientific claim must forbid something. Einstein's general relativity predicted that starlight passing the sun would bend by a specific amount, and a measurement of a different amount would have refuted it. That risk, Popper said, is what made it scientific, quite apart from whether it turned out to be true.

The criterion has been criticised as too strict. A failed prediction can often be blamed on an auxiliary assumption rather than the theory itself, and working scientists rarely abandon a productive theory on one bad result.

options: A sufficiently flexible theory can find support anywhere
questions.explanation: Popper argued a theory that explains any outcome will find support everywhere.

options: To give an example of a claim that forbade a specific outcome
To show general relativity is true
questions.explanation: The prediction could have been refuted by a different measurement, which is Popper's point.

options: It cannot be applied to astronomy
A failed prediction can be blamed on auxiliary assumptions
questions.explanation: The final paragraph notes this, along with scientists' reluctance to abandon productive theories.

title: How Bees Communicate Distance
text:
A returning honeybee performs a dance on the vertical comb that tells other foragers where she has fed. Direction is encoded by angle: the straight run of the dance departs from vertical by the same angle the food source departs from the sun.

Distance is encoded by duration, and here the bee is measuring something less obvious than metres. Experiments in which bees flew through narrow tunnels lined with patterns showed they overestimated distance badly, because the walls streamed past quickly. Bees flown through tunnels with plain walls underestimated it. What the bee reports is not distance travelled but the total visual motion that passed her eyes on the way.

The measure works because in open country visual flow and distance correlate closely. It fails precisely where an experimenter breaks that correlation.

depends on the position of the sun
questions.explanation: In open country visual flow and distance correlate closely, so the measure works.

title: Why Cities Grew by Rivers
text:
Before railways, water moved goods and land did not. A horse could haul perhaps a tonne over a road; the same horse on a towpath could pull thirty tonnes on a barge. Any settlement that needed to trade in bulk therefore grew where water was.

Rivers offered more than transport. They supplied drinking water, carried away waste, drove mills, and provided a defensible boundary. Sites at a river mouth, a ford, or the highest point a seagoing ship could reach were especially favoured, because goods had to change hands there and someone could tax the transfer.

Railways broke the dependence within a few decades, and later road freight broke it further. The pattern nonetheless persists, because a city once established is expensive to move.

options: Water transport was vastly more efficient than land transport
questions.explanation: The horse comparison establishes the efficiency gap as the central reason.

title: The Trouble with Averages
text:
An average is a summary, and every summary discards information. Which information it discards determines when it misleads.

The arithmetic mean is sensitive to extreme values. A room of ten people with modest incomes has a mean income that a single billionaire walking in would multiply many times over, though nine of the eleven people present are no better off. The median, the middle value, is unaffected by that entrant, which is why income statistics usually report it.

A subtler failure is averaging over groups that behave differently. If a treatment helps one group and harms another in equal measure, the average effect is zero and the honest conclusion, that the treatment matters a great deal, is exactly the one the summary hides.

options: It is always higher than the mean
It is unaffected by extreme values

title: Lascaux and the Question of Purpose
text:
The painted caves of southern France and northern Spain contain some of the oldest known art, and almost every claim about why they were made is contested. The images are overwhelmingly of large animals. Humans are rare, crudely drawn, and often incomplete.

One early interpretation held the paintings to be hunting magic, images made to secure success in the hunt. The pattern of species undercuts it: the animals eaten most often, judging by bones in occupation layers, are not the animals most often painted.

Other proposals treat the caves as places of ritual initiation, as records of myth, or as teaching aids. What can be said with confidence is narrower. The painters returned to the same chambers over long periods, worked deep underground by lamplight where no one lived, and took considerable trouble to do so.

options: The most eaten animals are not the most painted
questions.explanation: Bones in occupation layers show a mismatch between diet and depicted species.

questions.explanation: The final sentence lists exactly these observations as the secure conclusions.

title: The Antikythera Mechanism
text:
In 1901 sponge divers off the Greek island of Antikythera recovered a corroded lump of bronze from a first-century BCE shipwreck. It sat largely ignored for decades. X-ray and later computed tomography revealed at least thirty interlocking gears cut with triangular teeth.

The device modelled the heavens. Turning a handle advanced dials showing the positions of the sun and moon, the phase of the moon, the dates of eclipses and the four-year cycle of athletic games. One gear train reproduced the moon's varying speed across the sky using a pin-and-slot arrangement, a mechanical solution to an astronomical irregularity Greek astronomers had measured but could not explain.

Nothing of comparable complexity survives from the following fourteen centuries. Whether the mechanism was unique or merely the one example that happened to sink is unknown.

options: It contained at least thirty interlocking gears
It was made of iron rather than bronze
questions.explanation: X-ray and CT scanning revealed at least thirty gears with triangular teeth.

reduced the number of gears required
questions.explanation: It reproduced the moon's varying speed, an irregularity that had been measured but not explained.

Whether it was unique is unknown
It was certainly one of many
questions.explanation: The final sentence states this is unknown.

title: Convergent Evolution
text:
The eye of an octopus and the eye of a human are strikingly similar: a lens focuses light onto a layer of receptors inside a fluid-filled chamber. The two lineages last shared an ancestor that had nothing of the kind. Each arrived at the design independently, a pattern biologists call convergent evolution.

The details betray the separate origins. In the vertebrate eye the receptors face away from the light, and the nerve fibres leaving them must pass back through the retina, producing a blind spot. In the octopus the receptors face the light and the fibres leave behind them. There is no blind spot.

Convergence suggests that for some problems the space of workable solutions is narrow. It also demonstrates that similarity of form is not by itself evidence of common ancestry.

options: That vertebrate eyes are more advanced
That the two eyes evolved separately
questions.explanation: The differing arrangement of receptors and nerves reveals independent origins.

that all species share a recent ancestor
that workable solutions to some problems are few
questions.explanation: The passage says convergence suggests the space of workable solutions is narrow.

title: The Green Revolution
text:
Between the 1940s and the 1970s, wheat and rice yields in parts of Asia and Latin America rose several-fold. The central innovation was breeding: new dwarf varieties put their energy into grain rather than stalk, and their short stems did not collapse under a heavy head, which taller varieties did when heavily fertilised.

The varieties came as a package. High yields required fertiliser, reliable irrigation and pesticides, so the gains went disproportionately to farmers who could afford inputs and had access to water. Regions dependent on rain saw far less benefit.

Aggregate results were nonetheless dramatic. India shifted from importing grain to exporting it within two decades. The costs, depleted aquifers, salinisation from over-irrigation and a narrowing of crop genetic diversity, appeared later and remain.

They put energy into grain and did not collapse under fertiliser
questions.explanation: The passage says short stems put energy into grain and did not collapse under a heavy head.

title: Placebo and Its Limits
text:
Patients given an inert pill sometimes improve, and the effect is real enough that trials must control for it. What produces the improvement is less clear than the phrase placebo effect suggests.

Several processes are bundled together in the term. Many conditions improve on their own, and a patient enrolls when symptoms are at their worst, so the next measurement is likely to be better regardless of treatment. Patients also report symptoms differently to a doctor who has just treated them. Genuine physiological responses occur too: expectation of pain relief measurably increases the release of the body's own opioids.

The distinction matters because the first two mechanisms change what is reported while the third changes what happens. Placebos reliably relieve pain and nausea. They do not shrink tumours.

title: Why Languages Lose Cases
text:
Old English marked nouns for case: different endings signalled whether a noun was subject, object or possessor, and word order was correspondingly free. Modern English has almost none of this, keeping case only in pronouns, where he and him still differ.

One driver was phonetic. English stress falls early in the word, and unstressed final syllables erode over centuries. The endings that carried case information were exactly the syllables least likely to survive.

Once endings blurred, word order had to do the work, and once word order was doing the work the endings became redundant, which accelerated their loss. Contact with Old Norse, a related language with different endings but similar roots, is often thought to have hastened the process, since speakers could understand one another more easily by ignoring endings than by learning both sets.

options: Stress shifted to the end of words
questions.explanation: English stress falls early, so unstressed final syllables, which carried case, eroded.

word order and endings both grew more complex
questions.explanation: Blurred endings forced word order to carry the load, which made endings redundant.

options: Speakers understood each other better by ignoring endings
questions.explanation: Ignoring endings was easier than learning both sets.

title: The Physics of Skating
text:
The standard explanation for why ice is slippery is that pressure from the skate lowers the melting point and produces a film of water. The physics does not support it. A skater's weight on a blade lowers the melting point by a fraction of a degree, nowhere near enough to melt ice at typical rink temperatures.

Two better explanations operate together. Friction from the moving blade generates heat and melts a thin layer directly, which is why ice grows more slippery as you move faster. And the surface of ice is intrinsically disordered even well below freezing: the topmost molecules, bonded on one side only, remain mobile, forming a quasi-liquid layer that exists whether anything is standing on it or not.

The premelted layer explains why ice is slippery to a stationary shoe.

Rinks are kept too cold to skate on
The melting point drop is far too small
questions.explanation: A skater's weight lowers the melting point by only a fraction of a degree.

questions.explanation: The final sentence states exactly this.

title: The Colosseum and Roman Concrete
text:
Roman concrete has outlasted much of what came after it, and marine structures are the most striking case: harbour walls poured two thousand years ago stand while modern harbour concrete degrades within decades.

The recipe explains part of it. Romans mixed lime with volcanic ash, and the reaction produced a binder that continues to react with seawater rather than being attacked by it. Analysis has found crystals growing inside the ancient concrete that formed long after pouring, sealing cracks as they appeared.

Survivorship complicates the comparison. The Roman structures still standing are the ones that did not fail, and a great deal of Roman concrete has vanished. Modern concrete is also reinforced with steel, which the Romans lacked, and steel corrodes and splits the concrete around it. The ancient material lasts partly because it asks less of itself.

options: Its continuing reaction with seawater, sealing cracks
questions.explanation: Crystals forming long after pouring seal cracks as they appear.

Because surviving structures are the ones that did not fail
questions.explanation: Comparison is skewed because much Roman concrete has vanished.

questions.explanation: Steel corrodes and splits the concrete around it.

title: Migration and the Magnetic Sense
text:
Some birds navigate over thousands of kilometres, at night, in their first year, without a parent to follow. Several cues are combined, and one of them is the earth's magnetic field.

Evidence for the sense is strong. Birds held in cages orient in their migratory direction, and reverse it when an artificial field is reversed around them. The mechanism is less settled. One leading proposal involves cryptochrome, a light-sensitive protein in the retina, in which a magnetic field alters the lifetime of a short-lived pair of radicals and thus the chemical signal reaching the brain. This predicts, correctly, that the sense should depend on light.

A second candidate involves magnetite, an iron mineral found in some birds' tissue. The two are not exclusive, and evidence suggests different species may weight them differently.

options: Birds avoid areas with iron deposits
Birds follow their parents on first migration
Caged birds reverse orientation when the field is reversed
questions.explanation: Reversing an artificial field reverses the birds' orientation.

questions.explanation: The proposal correctly predicts that the sense should depend on light.

questions.explanation: The two are not exclusive and species may weight them differently.

title: The Invention of the Zero
text:
Zero entered mathematics twice, in two distinct roles. As a placeholder it is old: Babylonian scribes used a mark to show an empty position, so that sixty-one could be told from three thousand six hundred and one. That mark was punctuation rather than a number, and never stood alone.

Zero as a quantity, something that could be added, subtracted and reasoned about, appears in India by the seventh century, where Brahmagupta set out rules for arithmetic with it. His rules for addition and subtraction match modern practice; his treatment of division by zero does not, and the problem resisted a satisfactory answer for a further thousand years.

The distinction matters. A placeholder makes notation efficient. A number makes negative quantities and eventually algebra coherent.

options: One is Babylonian, the other Greek
One is written, the other spoken
One is used in arithmetic, the other in geometry
One marks an empty position, the other is a quantity to reason about
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts placeholder punctuation with zero as an operable number.

matched modern practice except for division
questions.explanation: His addition and subtraction rules match; his treatment of division by zero does not.

options: Zero is not a real number
A number makes negatives and algebra coherent
questions.explanation: The final sentence gives exactly this contrast.

title: Why Deserts Form Where They Do
text:
The great deserts cluster around thirty degrees north and south, and the pattern is atmospheric rather than accidental. Air heated at the equator rises, sheds its moisture as rain, and travels poleward at altitude. Around thirty degrees it descends, and descending air warms and takes up moisture rather than releasing it. The result is a belt of dry, stable air.

Two other mechanisms produce deserts elsewhere. A mountain range forces air upward, which rains on the windward slope and descends dry on the other, leaving a rain shadow. And a cold ocean current along a coast chills the air above it, suppressing the convection that would otherwise carry moisture inland, which is why the Atacama sits beside an ocean and receives almost no rain.

Distance from any ocean produces a fourth kind.

It moves too quickly to collect moisture
It is colder than surrounding air
It has already lost moisture and warms as it sinks
questions.explanation: Air sheds moisture at the equator, and descending air warms and takes up moisture instead of releasing it.

options: it is far from any ocean

a mountain range blocks the sea
questions.explanation: A cold current chills the air and suppresses the convection that would carry moisture inland.

options: air rains on a windward slope and descends dry
a coast faces a warm current
questions.explanation: That is the described mechanism.

title: Photography and Painting
text:
When photography became practical in the 1840s, portrait painters lost much of their trade almost at once. A likeness that had taken sittings and a substantial fee could be had in minutes for a fraction of the cost.

The usual account holds that painting responded by abandoning representation, and that impressionism and what followed were made possible by photography relieving painting of the duty to record. There is something to this, though the chronology is loose and painters had been moving in that direction already.

A subtler influence ran the other way. Early photographs, with their long exposures, blurred anything that moved and cropped figures arbitrarily at the frame edge. Painters began to imitate those accidents deliberately, and the off-centre composition and cut-off figure entered painting from the camera rather than the other way round.

questions.explanation: The passage summarises the usual account as photography relieving painting of the duty to record.

questions.explanation: Off-centre composition and cut-off figures entered painting from the camera.

title: Fermentation and Food Preservation
text:
Fermentation preserves food by making it inhospitable. Bacteria or yeasts consume the sugars present and produce acid or alcohol, and the resulting environment stops most spoilage organisms from growing. Cabbage becomes sauerkraut when lactic acid bacteria drop its acidity below the point where competitors survive.

The method is old, widespread and was arrived at independently in most inhabited regions, which is unsurprising given that it requires no equipment and happens spontaneously in the right conditions. What varies is control. Salt regulates which organisms flourish, temperature sets the pace, and excluding air favours the organisms that do not need it.

Fermentation also changes food beyond preserving it. It breaks down compounds that are hard to digest, produces vitamins absent in the raw material, and generates flavours that no fresh ingredient contains.

By sealing food from air permanently

title: The Broken Windows Debate
text:
In 1982 two social scientists proposed that visible disorder, broken windows, graffiti, uncollected rubbish, signals that a neighbourhood is unmonitored, and that the signal invites more serious crime. The policy conclusion drawn was that attending to minor disorder would prevent major offences.

Several cities adopted the approach, and crime fell in the following years. Whether the policy caused the fall is disputed, because crime fell in cities that adopted it and cities that did not, over the same period, which points to some common cause.

Field experiments give the underlying psychology partial support: people litter more in an already littered environment. But the step from that finding to a policing strategy is long, and critics argue the strategy in practice concentrated enforcement on minor offences in poor neighbourhoods without touching the causes of serious crime.

That crime is caused by poverty alone
That graffiti is a form of art

questions.explanation: Crime fell in both adopting and non-adopting cities, suggesting a common cause.

That disorder has no effect on behaviour

title: Why We Forget
text:
Forgetting is often treated as a failure of memory, but the evidence suggests it is partly a function of it. A system that retained everything would have to search everything, and relevance would be buried in detail.

Some forgetting is decay, a trace weakening when it is not used. More is interference. New learning competes with old: a person who has moved house repeatedly recalls the current address readily and the previous ones poorly, not because the older traces have vanished but because the newer ones win the competition to be retrieved.

Retrieval itself is selective in a way that shapes what remains. Recalling one item actively suppresses related items that compete with it, so the act of remembering one thing makes neighbouring things harder to reach. Memory is edited by use, not merely worn away by time.

questions.explanation: Recalling one item actively suppresses related competitors.

title: Containerisation
text:
Before the 1960s, loading a ship meant handling cargo piece by piece. Gangs of dockers moved barrels, sacks and crates into holds, a ship might spend longer in port than at sea, and loading could account for a substantial share of the cost of shipping a good.

The shipping container removed the handling. A sealed steel box could be filled inland, lifted by crane, stacked, and moved to a lorry or railcar without being opened. Port time collapsed from weeks to hours and costs fell by an order of magnitude.

The consequences reached far beyond ports. When moving a good across an ocean costs little, manufacturing can be sited far from where products are sold, and supply chains can be split across continents. Container shipping did not cause globalisation on its own, but little of it would have been affordable without it.

It was neither necessary nor important
questions.explanation: The final sentence makes exactly this qualified claim.

title: Bird Song and Dialect
text:
A white-crowned sparrow raised in silence produces a crude, unstructured song. Raised where it can hear adults of its species during a limited window in its first months, it produces the full song of its region, and the regions differ enough that a trained listener can place a bird within a few kilometres.

The learning is constrained. A sparrow exposed to the song of another species during the same window does not learn it. The bird appears to arrive with a template specific enough to reject the wrong model and loose enough to absorb local variation within the right one.

The parallel with human language is close but should not be pushed far. Song serves narrow functions, chiefly attracting mates and defending territory, and cannot be recombined to express anything new.

It produces a crude, unstructured song
It produces no song at all

The learning window is very long

title: The Library of Alexandria
text:
The Library of Alexandria is usually remembered for its destruction, and the story is generally told as a single catastrophe. The evidence suggests something slower and less dramatic.

Caesar's troops burned part of the harbour district in 48 BCE and probably destroyed a warehouse of scrolls. The Museum survived. Later centuries brought civil conflict, the withdrawal of royal patronage that had paid for copying and acquisition, and the gradual departure of scholars to other cities.

A library is not only a building. It is a budget, a staff of copyists, and a network that finds and reproduces texts, and papyrus decays within a few centuries in the Egyptian climate unless continually recopied. Once the funding stopped, the collection was dying whether or not anything burned. Institutions of this kind usually end by neglect rather than by fire.

options: Papyrus is more durable than parchment
The library declined gradually rather than in one catastrophe
questions.explanation: The passage argues for a slower decline through lost funding and departing scholars.

title: Antibiotic Resistance
text:
Resistance is not caused by antibiotics; it is revealed by them. In any large bacterial population a few individuals carry mutations that happen to blunt a drug's effect. Treatment kills the susceptible majority and leaves those few to multiply without competition.

Bacteria also trade resistance directly. Genes conferring it often sit on plasmids, small rings of DNA that can pass between cells and even between species, so resistance acquired in one population can appear in an unrelated one without descent.

The practical consequences follow from the mechanism. Finishing a course matters because a partial course may leave the least susceptible survivors. Using antibiotics for viral infections applies selection pressure with no possible benefit. And agricultural use, where drugs are given routinely to healthy animals, maintains that pressure on an enormous scale.

title: Cartography and Projection
text:
Every flat map of the earth is wrong, and necessarily so. A sphere cannot be laid flat without stretching, so a projection must choose which property to preserve and which to sacrifice.

Mercator preserves angles. A course of constant compass bearing appears as a straight line, which is why it became the navigator's map and why it survives on screens today. The cost is area: land near the poles is inflated enormously, and Greenland appears comparable to Africa when Africa is fourteen times larger.

Equal-area projections such as Gall-Peters preserve relative size and distort shape instead, stretching continents into unfamiliar outlines. Neither is more correct. The relevant question is what the map is for, and a projection that answers one purpose well will answer another badly.

questions.explanation: The relevant question is what the map is for.

title: Volcanic Winters
text:
A large eruption can cool the planet, but not through ash, which falls out within weeks. The agent is sulphur dioxide injected into the stratosphere, where it forms fine sulphate droplets that reflect sunlight and remain aloft for a year or more.

The eruption of Tambora in 1815 produced the following year without a summer. Snow fell in New England in June, harvests failed across Europe, and grain prices rose steeply. The connection was not understood at the time and was reconstructed much later from ice cores, which preserve the sulphate signal in datable layers.

Height matters more than size. An eruption that spreads ash widely but does not reach the stratosphere has little climatic effect, while a smaller eruption that punches through has a disproportionate one.

questions.explanation: Height matters more than size; reaching the stratosphere is decisive.

title: The Sunk Cost Fallacy
text:
A rational decision about whether to continue a project depends only on its future costs and benefits. Money already spent cannot be recovered by continuing, so it should not enter the calculation. People nonetheless weigh it heavily.

In a well-known demonstration, participants who had paid for a theatre ticket were more likely to attend in a snowstorm than participants given the same ticket free. The discomfort of the journey and the value of the performance were identical; only the irrecoverable payment differed.

Explanations vary. The behaviour may reflect an aversion to appearing wasteful, or a reluctance to admit an earlier decision was mistaken. Whatever the cause, it scales: governments and firms continue failing projects for the reason that so much has already been spent, which is the one consideration that should carry no weight at all.

questions.explanation: Money already spent cannot be recovered by continuing.

The cost of travel in snow

questions.explanation: It notes the reason cited is precisely the one that should carry no weight.

title: Terracing and Soil
text:
Farming a steep slope invites erosion. Rain running downhill carries topsoil with it, and topsoil is the layer that holds nutrients and water. A field can lose in one storm what took centuries to accumulate.

Terracing answers this by cutting the slope into a staircase of level platforms held by walls or banks. Water reaching a terrace slows, spreads and soaks in rather than running off, and the soil stays where it is. Systems in the Andes and in the rice-growing regions of East and Southeast Asia have been cultivated continuously for many centuries.

The requirement is maintenance. A terrace wall that fails concentrates water on the terrace below and can trigger a cascade, so terraced landscapes tend to be abandoned all at once rather than gradually when the labour to maintain them disappears.

title: Why Metals Conduct
text:
In most solids the electrons are held to particular atoms. In a metal the outermost electrons are not: they occupy states spread through the whole crystal and move freely, which is why a metal conducts electricity and heat and why it is shiny, since mobile electrons re-emit the light that strikes them.

Resistance comes from the lattice. A perfectly regular array of atoms would not scatter the electrons at all, but atoms vibrate with heat, and the vibrations disturb the regularity. Heating a metal therefore increases its resistance, which is the opposite of what happens in a semiconductor, where heating frees additional carriers and conductivity rises.

Cooling towards absolute zero reduces vibration and resistance falls, and in some materials it vanishes entirely below a critical temperature, a separate phenomenon with a different explanation.

questions.explanation: Vibrations disturb the regularity, scattering electrons.

title: The Printing Press and Standard Spelling
text:
English spelling was once flexible. A scribe wrote as he heard, and the same word might appear several ways on one page without anyone objecting.

Printing changed the economics. A printer setting type wanted a single form to reuse, compositors were often trained on the same texts, and printed books circulated far beyond the region where they were set, so one region's forms spread. Spelling settled towards a standard within roughly a century and a half.

The timing was unfortunate. The standard fixed during and just after a period of rapid change in English pronunciation, and spelling stopped moving while speech continued. That is why knight retains letters for sounds that were pronounced when the spelling was set and have since disappeared, and why English spelling records a pronunciation that no living speaker uses.

options: A single form could be reused and set more efficiently
questions.explanation: A printer setting type wanted a single form to reuse.

title: Cooperative Hunting
text:
Several predators hunt in groups, but grouping alone is not cooperation. Wolves and lions often simply converge on the same prey, each acting for itself, and the apparent coordination is a by-product.

Stricter evidence requires individuals taking different roles. Some lionesses reliably circle to drive prey while others wait in ambush, and they keep those roles across hunts. Harris's hawks hunt in relays, one flushing prey from cover while others wait above.

Cooperation raises a problem it does not solve: a group member that contributes nothing still eats. Where this has been examined, the answer is usually that participation is observable and that non-participants are tolerated less. The mechanism sustaining cooperation is therefore rarely generosity, and usually the cost of being seen not to help.

questions.explanation: Stricter evidence requires individuals taking different roles and keeping them.

options: A member that contributes nothing still eats

questions.explanation: The mechanism is rarely generosity and usually the cost of being seen not to help.

title: Glass and the Telescope
text:
The telescope required a material problem to be solved before an optical one. Useful lenses need glass that is clear, free of bubbles and uniform in density, and for most of history glass was none of these.

Venetian glassmakers on Murano developed cristallo in the fifteenth century, a soda glass of unusual clarity, and their techniques spread despite determined efforts to keep them secret. By the early seventeenth century, glass adequate for grinding into lenses was available across northern Europe, and the telescope appeared in the Netherlands in 1608 in the hands of spectacle makers rather than astronomers.

Galileo heard a description, built his own within months and improved it, and turned it upward. The instrument that reshaped astronomy was, in its origins, a by-product of the spectacle trade.

title: Measuring Unemployment
text:
An unemployment rate looks like a simple count and is not. The standard definition counts people without work who are available for work and have actively sought it recently, which excludes two large groups.

The first is discouraged workers, who want a job but have stopped looking because they expect to find none. They leave the labour force by definition, and their departure lowers the measured rate. A recession deep enough to discourage people can therefore improve the headline figure.

The second is the underemployed: part-time workers who want full-time hours, and people in jobs far below their qualifications. Both count as employed.

Statistical agencies publish broader measures alongside the headline for exactly this reason, though the headline is the number that gets reported.

title: Symbiosis in the Soil
text:
Most land plants are joined at the root to fungi, in a partnership called mycorrhiza that is older than forests and probably older than roots. The fungus threads through soil far finer than any root can penetrate and delivers phosphorus and water to the plant. The plant, which can photosynthesise and the fungus cannot, returns sugars.

The exchange is not automatic charity. Experiments in which one partner is starved show the other reduces its contribution, and plants direct more sugar to fungal strands that deliver more phosphorus. The relationship is regulated, and each side responds to what it receives.

Because a single fungal network may connect many plants, resources can move between individuals through it, though how much of this reflects deliberate transfer rather than leakage remains debated.

options: The plant supplies water; the fungus supplies sugars
The fungus supplies phosphorus and water; the plant supplies sugars
questions.explanation: The fungus delivers phosphorus and water, the plant returns sugars.

title: The Cost of Monumental Building
text:
Monumental construction is expensive in a way that looks irrational. Moving stones weighing many tonnes without wheels or draught animals, as at Stonehenge or on Rapa Nui, consumed labour that could have produced food.

Several explanations have been offered. Monuments may coordinate: a project requiring hundreds of workers for years demands organisation, and the organisation may outlast the project. They may signal, since a society able to waste labour on this scale advertises a surplus and, implicitly, a capacity to defend it. They may also simply be what the labour was for, in societies where obligation to work on communal projects was the form taxation took.

What the explanations share is a refusal to treat the cost as waste. The expense is not incidental to the monument's function; in each account it is the function.

How ancient people moved heavy stones

title: Reading the Ice
text:
An ice sheet is an archive. Snow falling on Antarctica or Greenland compacts into ice without melting, and each year's layer traps a sample of the atmosphere in bubbles along with dust, ash and pollen. Drilling a core and counting downward reads the record backwards, in places for more than 800,000 years.

The bubbles are the crucial part, because they hold actual ancient air rather than a proxy for it. Carbon dioxide and methane can be measured directly, and the isotopic composition of the ice itself indicates the temperature at which the snow formed.

The correlation between the two records is close, which is what makes the archive so consequential. Whether temperature drove gas concentration or the reverse cannot be settled from correlation alone, and the ordering has occupied researchers for decades.

options: They contain actual ancient air rather than a proxy
questions.explanation: The passage stresses they hold actual ancient air, allowing direct measurement.

The depth of the ice sheet
questions.explanation: Isotopic composition indicates formation temperature.

options: Which of temperature and gas concentration drove the other

title: The Metric of Musical Time
text:
A metronome divides time into identical intervals, but performed music rarely follows one. Measurements of pianists playing the same phrase repeatedly show consistent departures from the printed values, and the departures are not random: notes at phrase endings are lengthened, and the lengthening scales with how important the ending is.

Listeners depend on these deviations. A recording quantised to exact mechanical timing is reliably described as lifeless, and listeners asked to locate phrase boundaries in such a version perform worse than with the unquantised original.

The deviations therefore carry structural information rather than merely decorating it. What notation records is a skeleton, and a performer supplies a layer of timing that tells the listener how the piece is organised.

options: Departures from printed timing are consistent and patterned
questions.explanation: The departures are described as consistent and not random.

questions.explanation: Listeners locate phrase boundaries worse without the deviations.

title: Salt and the State
text:
Salt preserves food, and before refrigeration a society without it could not store a harvest or provision an army. Because everyone needed it and it was produced in few places, it was unusually easy to tax.

States exploited this for millennia. China operated a salt monopoly from the seventh century BCE, and at times the revenue approached half the imperial budget. France's gabelle required households to buy a fixed quantity at a set price, with rates differing so sharply between provinces that smuggling across internal borders became a substantial occupation.

The economics of a salt tax explain its politics. A good that people must buy regardless of price yields steady revenue, and for the same reason takes a larger share of a poor household's income than a rich one's, which is why salt taxes recur so often in the history of revolt.

options: Everyone needed it and it came from few places
It was used only by the wealthy
questions.explanation: Universal need plus concentrated production made it easy to tax.

title: Camouflage and Counter-Shading
text:
An animal lit from above is bright on top and shadowed underneath, and that gradient betrays its shape even when its colour matches the background. Counter-shading cancels it: the animal is dark above and pale below, so illumination and pigmentation offset each other and the body reads as flat.

The pattern appears in fish, birds, mammals and even some caterpillars, and where a caterpillar habitually hangs upside down the shading is reversed to match. That reversal is strong evidence the pattern is functional rather than incidental.

Counter-shading fails in flat light. Under an overcast sky, with no strong gradient to cancel, a counter-shaded animal is slightly conspicuous, which is one reason many species combine it with disruptive markings that break the outline by a different mechanism.

By cancelling the light gradient that reveals shape
By reflecting light away from the observer
By matching the background colour exactly
questions.explanation: Dark above and pale below offsets illumination so the body reads as flat.

options: It is caused by their habitat
It shows the pattern is functional
questions.explanation: Reversal to match an upside-down posture is evidence of function rather than accident.

title: Why Bridges Fall
text:
The Tacoma Narrows bridge collapsed in 1940, and the event is often explained as resonance, with the wind supposedly matching the bridge's natural frequency. That account is wrong, and the correct one is more interesting.

Resonance requires a periodic driving force at a fixed frequency. The wind that day was steady, not oscillating. What occurred was aeroelastic flutter: the deck's own twisting altered how air flowed around it, and the altered flow pushed the deck further in the direction it was already twisting. The motion supplied its own driving force, and the amplitude grew until the structure failed.

The distinction matters for design. A resonance problem is solved by shifting the natural frequency away from expected inputs. A flutter problem cannot be, because the structure generates the input, and must be addressed by changing the shape so the airflow no longer feeds the motion.

options: The bridge had no natural frequency
The wind was steady rather than oscillating
questions.explanation: Resonance needs a periodic driving force; the wind that day was steady.

options: the structure's own motion altering the airflow
questions.explanation: The deck's twisting altered the flow, which pushed it further in the same direction.

questions.question: Why can a flutter problem not be solved by shifting the natural frequency?
options: The structure generates the input itself
questions.explanation: Because the structure supplies its own driving force, shifting frequency does not help.

title: The Spice Trade and Navigation
text:
Pepper, cloves and nutmeg were worth carrying across the world because they were light, durable and enormously marked up. Cloves and nutmeg grew on a handful of islands in eastern Indonesia, and every kilogram sold in Europe had passed through many hands, each adding a margin.

The prize was therefore not the spice but the route. A European power reaching the islands directly could buy at source and cut out the chain. This is what funded the voyages of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, and what made the resulting maps state secrets: a chart showing safe passage was worth more than a cargo.

The outcome was self-limiting. Once several powers held the route, the margin collapsed, and the trading companies built to exploit scarcity found themselves competing on volume instead.

They were light, durable and heavily marked up

options: The margin collapsed and competition shifted to volume
questions.explanation: The outcome was self-limiting: margins collapsed and companies competed on volume.

title: Enzymes and Temperature
text:
An enzyme speeds a reaction by holding the reacting molecules in a particular arrangement, and that arrangement depends on the enzyme's folded shape. The dependence produces a characteristic curve when activity is plotted against temperature.

Warming initially helps. Molecules move faster, collisions are more frequent, and reaction rate rises much as it would without an enzyme. Beyond an optimum the curve falls steeply, because the bonds maintaining the fold begin to break and the shape is lost. The enzyme does not become slow so much as cease to be an enzyme.

The optimum tracks the organism. Enzymes from bacteria living in hot springs retain their fold above eighty degrees, and enzymes from Antarctic fish work at temperatures where mammalian enzymes are nearly inert. The chemistry is the same; the stability of the fold differs.

title: Public Transport and Density
text:
A transport system's viability depends less on technology than on how many people live within walking distance of it. A tram line through dense housing draws riders from every stop; the same line through detached suburbs draws few, because the walk to the stop is long and most trips begin somewhere the line does not serve.

The relationship runs both ways. Where transit exists first, development tends to cluster around stations, since land there becomes more valuable. Where roads come first, development spreads thinly, and thin development cannot afterwards support transit without subsidy.

This is why retrofitting is so difficult. The pattern of a city is set early and lasts for a century or more, and a transit line added to a low-density landscape is competing against a geometry that was fixed long before it arrived.

title: The Antibody Repertoire
text:
The immune system must recognise pathogens it has never encountered, including ones that do not yet exist. It cannot carry a gene for every possible antibody, since the number required exceeds the number of genes in the genome by many orders of magnitude.

The solution is combinatorial. Antibody genes are stored as separate segments, and each developing B cell cuts and rejoins a selection of them at random, adding further variation at the junctions. A modest library of segments therefore generates an enormous number of distinct receptors.

Randomness creates a hazard: some receptors will recognise the body's own tissue. Developing cells are therefore tested against self-molecules and those that bind strongly are eliminated or edited. The system generates diversity blindly and then removes what is dangerous, rather than designing what is useful.

title: Loanwords and Prestige
text:
When two languages meet, words move, and the direction is rarely symmetrical. English absorbed thousands of French words after 1066, while French took comparatively few from English at the time. The asymmetry tracked power rather than any property of the languages.

The domains borrowed reveal the relationship. English kept its own words for the animals a farmer raised, cow, sheep, swine, and took French words for the meat served at table, beef, mutton, pork. Words for law, government and cuisine came in bulk; words for weather, family and the body largely did not.

Borrowing therefore records who controlled which spheres of life. A vocabulary is in part a sedimentary deposit, and the layers can be read.

options: The relative power of the groups
